content: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a gas that is colorless, odorless, tasteless, and non-irritating. It becomes toxic to humans when its concentration exceeds 100 parts per million (ppm). Causes of Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Life-Threatening Causes Life-threatening causes of carbon monoxide poisoning are those that can result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours if left untreated. Death can occur from nearly all causes of CO poisoning, depending on the levels of carbon monoxide in the blood. Boats and motor vehicles. Charcoal grills, propane stoves, and charcoal briquettes. Gas-powered generators. Fires involving electrical cables. Situations immediately following hurricanes or other natural disasters. Malfunctioning heating systems. Gas-powered tools such as power washers. Management of Acute Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Recommended Actions (Do's) Evaluate all potential high-risk factors and initiate treatment with hyperbaric oxygen therapy when indicated. Administer hyperbaric oxygen therapy to pregnant women regardless of the severity of carbon monoxide poisoning. Provide 100% oxygen therapy until the patient is free of symptoms, with a minimum duration of 4-5 hours. Warn all patients about the possibility of delayed neurological complications. Perform a chest X-ray in all cases of severe poisoning. Additionally, consider conducting an electrocardiogram (EKG), troponin tests, and, in some cases, advanced imaging such as CT or MRI. Schedule a follow-up visit for the patient within two weeks. Patients with mild symptoms may be safely discharged from the emergency department once they are symptom-free. Actions to Avoid (Don'ts) Do not rely solely on carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) levels, as they are not always reliable. Instead, correlate these levels with the patient’s clinical symptoms. Do not use standard pulse oximetry, as it is not effective in detecting carbon monoxide poisoning. Do not neglect to perform a pregnancy test on all women of childbearing age.
